newsitem.title: USA: IMF chief opposes EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: IMF chief opposes EMU delay.

text.p: The head of the International Monetary Fund came out on Tuesday against any delay in the planned 1999 launch of a new European currency, saying it was time "to finish the job" of monetary union.

In a speech for delivery to an IMF-sponsored conference here, Managing Director Michel Camdessus suggested that the tough 1997 budget criteria set down in the Maastricht Treaty for the launch of the euro could be interpreted flexibly to allow the ambitious project to go ahead.

"In the final analysis ... the most important thing is to ensure that the underlying pace of fiscal consolidation is adequate, and, above all, that countries' commitments beyond 1997 are consistent with the Maastricht Treaty," he said.

Financial markets have been abuzz with rumors that the start of european monetary union (EMU) will be delayed because of the difficulties that many nations, particularly Germany, face in meeting the Maastricht budget criteria for this year.
Under the Treaty, nations that wish to join the union must reduce their budget deficits this year to about the equivalent of three percent of gross domestic product.

"The Treaty offers some scope for interpretation," Camdessus said in an apparent suggestion that countries might be allowed to narrowly miss the three percent target this year if their long-term budget plans were sound.
The IMF chief said it was "feasible" that most European countries will hit the three percent target for this year.
"There are good grounds for believing that growth will be stronger this year than last and that countries' budgetary positions will improve," he said.
But if economic growth looks to be falling short of expectations, Camdessus suggested that European nations should consider cutting interest rates to help boost output.

"If there were a need to support economic activity -- while inflation remains subdued and fiscal consolidation was proceeding -- an easing of monetary conditions might be considered," the IMF chief said.
He stressed the importance of the EMU beginning on a "sound economic footing" -- both for those who qualify to join at the start and for those who will participate later.
"Later entrance must ... help ensure that EMU begins on time, and with an appropriate initial size -- but most importantly, that it begins on a sound economic footing," he said.
"The essential thing," he added, "is that a clear road map be established for them (the later entrants) to join as soon as possible thereafter, so that there are no adverse market reactions."
Camdessus acknowledged that currency markets might be more prone to misalignments after the introduction of the Euro and highlighted the role that the IMF can play in dealing with them.
"The incidences of misalignments could become more frequent and more damaging in a bi- or tri-polar (currency regime)," the IMF chief said.
He also warned that persistent high European unemployment could undermine the credibility of the Euro as a stable currency and urged European countries to do more to reform their labor markets.
"Progress in addressing labor market rigidities has been painfully slow in most EU (European Union) countries," Camdessus said. "Much more determined action is needed."
